subject: Creativity
title: Divergent Thinking: Generating Many Ideas
description: A micro-lesson that makes Divergent Thinking: Generating Many Ideas usable.

hook.text: Ask a child how many uses a paperclip has. They'll give 200. Ask an adult. They'll give 10. What happened?

buildup.text: J.P. Guilford coined 'divergent thinking' in 1967 — the ability to generate many different ideas from one prompt.

discovery.text: It's measured by fluency (how many), flexibility (how different), and originality (how unusual) your ideas are.

twist.text: Schools systematically reduce divergent thinking. 98% of kindergarteners score as 'genius-level.' By adulthood: only 2%.

climax.text: The good news: divergent thinking can be retrained. It's a skill, not a talent. Practice brings it back.

punchline.text: You were born a divergent-thinking genius. School trained it out.

quiz.question: What three metrics measure divergent thinking?

details.summary: Divergent thinking is the ability to generate many different ideas from a single starting point. It values quantity over quality, fluency over perfection, and wild ideas over safe ones. It is the expansion phase of any creative process.
details.whyItMatters: Divergent thinking is the most trainable component of creativity. Practicing it consistently increases creative output, and it forms the foundation of brainstorming and ideation techniques.
takeaways: Divergent thinking prioritizes quantity and variety of ideas
Judgment must be suspended during divergent thinking
It can be measured and improved through deliberate practice

faq.question: How do you improve divergent thinking?
faq.answer: Practice alternative uses exercises, word association games, and timed idea generation challenges. The key is volume without judgment. Research shows that people who regularly practice divergent thinking become measurably more creative over time.

faq.question: Is divergent thinking the same as brainstorming?
faq.answer: Divergent thinking is the cognitive skill; brainstorming is one technique that uses it. Other techniques like mind mapping, free writing, and SCAMPER also rely on divergent thinking as their underlying mental process.
